etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English vice, from Old French vice, from Latin vitium (“fault or blemish”). Displaced native Old English unþēaw.

quote.citation: 2008, BioWare, Mass Effect (Science Fiction), Redwood City: Electronic Arts, →ISBN, →OCLC, PC, scene: Noveria:
quote.text: Shepard: I wear a lot of hats, Mr. Vargas. Some days I shut down criminals. Some days I defuse nukes. Some days I like to enjoy private vices. You understand me?
It's a rush you can't deny / A little violence is the ultimate drug / Let's get high / You've been powerless to your vices / Self-control defies you

quote.citation: 2022 October 21, Taylor Swift, Jack Antonoff, “Anti-Hero”, in Midnights‎[1], performed by Taylor Swift:
quote.text: I should not be left to my own devices / they come with prices and vices / I end up in crisis / Tale as old as time

definitions.definition: (law) Any of various crimes related (depending on jurisdiction) to weapons, prostitution, pornography, gambling, alcohol, tobacco, or drugs.
(law enforcement, slang) Clipping of vice squad.
A defect in the temper or behaviour of a horse, such as to make the animal dangerous, to injure its health, or to diminish its usefulness.

quote.citation: 1839, Scholefield v. Robb; cited in Gilligan, Brenda, Practical Horse Law‎[2], 2002, →ISBN:
quote.text: So a horse with say, navicular disease, making him suitable only for light hacking, would probably be unsound, whereas rearing would be a vice, being a "defect in the temper... making it dangerous". A vice can however render a horse unsound - possibly a crib biter will damage its wind.

definitions.definition: (UK) Alternative spelling of vise (“mechanical screw apparatus used for clamping”)
A tool for drawing lead into cames, or flat grooved rods, for casements.

quote.citation: c. 1596–1599 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Second Part of Henry the Fourth, […]”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene i], page 79, line 22:
quote.text: Fang. If I but fiſt him once: if he come but within my Vice.

definitions.definition: Alternative spelling of vise (“to hold or squeeze with a vice”)

quote.citation: c. 1610–1611 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Winters Tale”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene ii], page 281, line 416:
quote.text: Camillo. As he had ſeen’t, or beene an Instrument / To vice you to't, that you haue toucht his Queene / Forbiddenly.

quote.citation: 1849 December, Thomas De Quincey, “The English Mail-coach. Section the Second.—The Vision of Sudden Death.”, in Miscellanies (De Quincey’s Works; IV), London: James Hogg & Sons, →OCLC, page 335:
quote.text: What could be done—who was it that could do it—to check the storm-flight of these maniacal horses? Could I not seize the reins from the slumbering coachman?  […]  [F]rom the way in which the coachman's hand was viced between his upper and lower thigh, this was impossible.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Latin vice (“in place of”), ablative form of vicis. Compare French fois (“time”) and Spanish vez (“time, turn”).

definitions.definition: in place of; subordinate to; designating a person below another in rank
(chiefly dated) Instead of; in place of; versus.

quote.citation: 1848 November – 1850 December, William Makepeace Thackeray, chapter XXI, in The History of Pendennis. […], volume I, London: Bradbury and Evans, […], published 1849, →OCLC:
quote.text: He was gardener and out-door man, vice Upton, resigned.

quote.citation: 1848 November – 1850 December, William Makepeace Thackeray, chapter XXVIII, in The History of Pendennis. […], volume I, London: Bradbury and Evans, […], published 1849, →OCLC:
quote.text: A very small cab-boy, vice Stoopid retired, swung on behind Foker's vehicle; knock-kneed and in the tightest leather breeches.

definitions.definition: One who acts in place of a superior.

quote.citation: c. 1850s-1870s, Edward Minister and Son, The Gazette of Fashion and Cutting-Room Companion
quote.text: The health of the Vice was proposed in appropriate language; in replying, Mr. Marriott thanked the company  […]
